title: S&P500, Nasdaq End Higher, Dow Hits Record High On Strong Mag 7 Performance And Falling Oil Prices — BA, XOM, CVX, HOOD, AMD In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock indices ended higher on Monday, with the S&P 500 shy of hitting record highs, tracking gains in big tech stocks, cooling oil prices, and easing bond yields. The S&P 500 ended 1.5% higher, while the Nasdaq 100 rose 1.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average ended 1.3% higher. The Russell 2000, which tracks stocks with small market capitalizations, jumped 1.8%. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) added 1.5%, and Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended Monday 1.9% higher, while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) rose 1.4%. Meanwhile, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) rose 1%, amid gains in Nvidia (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO) and Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). The broader Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT) added 2%, tracking gains in Magnificent Seven stocks. The Roundhill Mag 7 ETF (MAGS) soared 3.5%. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY and QQQ was ‘bearish’ and ‘neutral’ for the DIA, with ‘high’ message volumes. Geopolitics once again took center stage in Monday’s trading session amid signs of easing tension between the U.S. and Iran after President Trump, over the weekend, canceled plans to attack the country. International Brent crude futures fell 4.73% to end at $83.77 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate futures settled down 5.11% at $80.34 per barrel. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield slid almost 6 basis points to about 4.688%. “Investors are keeping their enthusiasm in check as ‘we’ve been here before,’ and it’s likely the conflict has further to go before reaching a resolution (if it ever does),” wrote Vital Knowledge founder Adam Crisafulli in a note accessed by CNBC. With earnings season underway, investor attention seems to be on corporate performance and management commentary. “Markets are transitioning from a flow-driven environment back to one increasingly dictated by earnings, corporate demand, and the macroeconomic backdrop,” Citadel Securities’s Scott Rubner wrote in a note. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration is set to rule on five closely watched treatments in August from Moderna, Lantheus Holdings, Bristol Myers Squibb, Capricor Therapeutics and Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical. Decisions are due by August 23 at the latest on therapies ranging from an mRNA flu vaccine to a gene therapy for a rare metabolic disorder, putting biotech investors on high alert as the outcomes could drive sharp near-term moves across the sector. Moderna is seeking approval for mRNA-1010, its experimental mRNA-based seasonal flu vaccine for adults 50 and older. An FDA advisory panel already voted unanimously in favor of the shot in June, and the FDA is slated to decide on its application by August 5. The FDA initially refused to file Moderna’s application in early February 2026, citing concerns that the comparator vaccine used in the main trial did not reflect the best available care for older adults. Moderna revised its plan, and now the company is seeking a traditional approval for adults aged 50-64 and an accelerated approval for adults 65 and older. If granted accelerated approval in the patient population, Moderna will be required to conduct another study to confirm effectiveness in the group. Lantheus wants approval for MK-6240, a PET imaging agent that detects tau protein tangles in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease. Doctors would use the scan to help confirm the presence of tau pathology, stage the disease, and guide treatment decisions. The FDA accepted the company’s application seeking approval in October and granted it a fast-track designation. The application is based on two late-stage trials in people with early Alzheimer’s disease. In both trials, the scan identified patients with tau pathology and ruled out people without it, to support the application. The FDA will decide on the application by August 13 at the latest. Bristol Myers Squibb is seeking approval for iberdomide, an oral drug combined with existing medicines for patients whose multiple myeloma has returned or stopped responding, by August 17. It works by helping the immune system attack cancer cells more effectively while also directly killing myeloma cells. Bristol Myers’ application was accepted by the FDA in February and granted priority review. The application relies on the large late-stage trial where iberdomide, together with Daratumumab and Dexamethasone, showed a statistically significant improvement in minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity rates compared to control arms. MRD negativity means no detectable cancer cells remain after treatment — an early sign of deep response. Capricor is seeking full approval for Deramiocel, a cell therapy aimed at heart damage caused by Duchenne muscular dystrophy. After an earlier rejection, the company submitted new data from its late-stage HOPE-3 trial to the FDA. However, in July, an advisory committee voted 9–3 against the claim that the available evidence provides substantial proof of effectiveness for treating DMD cardiomyopathy. The vote is non-binding, meaning the FDA could still approve the therapy. Ultragenyx is seeking approval for DTX401, a one-time gene therapy for glycogen storage disease type Ia, a rare inherited metabolic disorder, by August 23. People with GSDIa cannot release stored sugar from the liver, leading to dangerous drops in blood sugar (hypoglycemia) during fasting, excess glycogen buildup in the liver and kidneys, and other long-term complications. The FDA granted priority review to Ultragenyx’s application in February. There are currently no approved treatments that address the underlying cause of GSDIa. Novavax is scheduled to release its second-quarter 2026 financial results before the U.S. market opens on Thursday. According to data from Fiscal AI, the company is expected to report quarterly revenue of $52.06 million, down from $239.24 in the corresponding quarter of 2025. Loss per share is expected to come in at $0.38, compared to the profit of $0.62 recorded in Q2 2025. Novavax has moved away from trying to sell COVID vaccines on a large scale by itself. Instead, it is running a leaner operation that mainly licenses its proprietary Matrix-M adjuvant — a technology that helps vaccines work better — to larger drugmakers. A key example is the January 2026 non-exclusive deal with Pfizer. Novavax received $30-million upfront and could earn up to $500 million more in milestones plus royalties if Pfizer uses Matrix-M in up to two vaccine programs. The company has also signed material-transfer agreements with other firms and continues work on combination vaccines through partnerships, including with Sanofi. In the first quarter, Novavax reported total revenue of about $140 million, with product sales declining sharply year-over-year while licensing and royalty revenue grew. The company has guided for full-year 2026 adjusted total revenue of $230–$270 million. On Thursday, investors will look for updates on cash position, progress with Matrix-M deals, and how the leaner model is performing. The brokerage firm announced on Monday that customers can begin requesting shares in the initial public offering of Robinhood Ventures Fund II (RVII). The closed-end fund expects to price at $25 per share and begin trading on the New York Stock Exchange on August 13 under the symbol "RVII." The allocation request window for self-directed account holders closes August 12. HOOD stock gained 6% on Monday, breaking past four consecutive days of losses. Historically, early-stage venture capital has been restricted to institutional funds and accredited high-net-worth investors. By the time private tech companies went public on major exchanges, much of their early growth was already realized. RVII operates as a business development company—a specialized type of closed-end fund that invests directly in private entities while giving public investors exchange-traded daily liquidity. Unlike traditional private equity funds, RVII imposes no minimum income or asset requirements on buyers. "With Robinhood Ventures Fund II, retail investors no longer have to wait until a company's IPO to be part of an early growth journey," said Sarah Pinto, head of Robinhood Ventures. The fund debuts with an initial portfolio of 80 private companies and plans to review additional opportunities each quarter. Its strategy emphasizes seed-stage funding for businesses connected to Y Combinator, the renowned startup accelerator that has backed thousands of companies and produced numerous tech "unicorns." Rich Aberman, portfolio manager for RVII, emphasized that the goal is to make retail investor representation standard across seed and Series A cap tables as the fund scales. The move comes as private technology firms delay entering public markets. Industry data indicates the median time from funding to IPO has stretched from five years in 1999 to roughly 14 years today, leaving trillions of dollars in market valuation locked within private portfolios. While early-stage startup investing carries elevated risk, Robinhood executives noted the fund is designed to lower institutional barriers and broaden participation in high-potential growth sectors. Individual traders using the Robinhood app, as well as registered investment advisers on the TradePMR Fusion platform, can submit share allocation requests ahead of the offering. Robinhood Ventures, an SEC-registered investment adviser and subsidiary of Robinhood Markets, will manage the vehicle. Omeros Corporation said on Monday that U.S. Medicare officials have approved extra payments to hospitals that use its newly launched drug YARTEMLEA to treat a rare and often deadly complication of stem cell transplants. Shares of the company were trading 4% higher at the time of writing. Starting October 1, hospitals can receive up to about $287,000 more from Medicare for each qualifying patient under the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ new status for the therapy. The extra funds go straight to the hospitals to help cover the high cost of the new treatment. Omeros itself will still receive the same payment for the drug. YARTEMLEA is the only medicine approved in the United States for this transplant complication, known as TA-TMA. The condition damages small blood vessels and can be life-threatening, especially for the kidneys. About three in 10 patients who receive the more complex type of stem-cell transplant in the U.S. are covered by Medicare. Company CEO Gregory Demopulos said the decision should make it easier for hospitals to choose the drug based on what patients need, rather than worrying about the cost. YARTEMLEA reached the market earlier this year after winning FDA approval in late 2025. It is Omeros’ first commercial product and the main source of near-term revenue. The company is counting on growing sales of the drug to help fund the rest of its research pipeline, which includes longer-lasting versions of similar medicines, experimental cancer therapies, a potential treatment for cocaine addiction, and other programs aimed at hard-to-treat conditions. In the first quarter this year, after YARTEMLEA launch, Omeros reported net product sales of $9.9 million. Worries continued despite the U.S. government’s efforts to curtail rising prices, including planned fuel releases and changes to U.S. sanctions on Russian imported fuel. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in February, energy prices have been climbing steadily, boosting energy companies. Retail investors in Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) are floating multibillion-dollar buyout scenarios and steep share-price gains after CEO Angelos Stergiou marked the company’s 15th anniversary with a post about its “next chapter.” SLS stock jumped 5% on Monday to $10.49, snapping three straight losing sessions. In his LinkedIn post, Stergiou reflected on Sellas’ growth from a private startup into a public biotech advancing investigational cancer treatments GPS and SLS009. “Reaching 15 years isn't just about celebrating our history; it is about stepping into our next chapter with even greater focus, drive, and resolve,” he said. He acknowledged past setbacks and thanked shareholders, employees and trial participants, while reaffirming the company’s commitment to patients. “Our mission remains deeply personal, and our promise to the patients we aim to serve is steadfast. We look forward, God willing, to the best chapters that are still to be written with GPS and SLS009,” he added. One user said: “My opinion, Dr. Stergiou’s message was a master-class at reassuring EVERYONE that all is well.” A user also floated a minimum $40 billion valuation. Another user argued for a $50 billion valuation, calling a $247-per-share figure. A separate user proposed a $120 billion buyout scenario and also predicted a share price of $540-plus. Across bullish share-price predictions, including scenarios tied to clinical results, targets ranged from $100 to over $540. Discussing buyout news in case of favorable data, one user said: “If BO news post good data then there’s no stopping this beast (really no explanation required as it could go full berserker mode).” BO means buyout. Another user challenged the lofty valuations and said: “I will be so glad to get out of this ticker when it hits $15 again.” The CEO’s message comes as investors have been searching for potential deal signals in recent months. In June, a filing disclosed changes to executive severance arrangements, including lump-sum payment provisions for Stergiou. For CFO John Burns and chief development officer Dragan Cicic, qualifying departures within one month before or one year after a change of control would trigger 15 months of salary, the annual target bonus, up to 18 months of health-coverage reimbursements and full vesting of unvested equity. Sellas’ conference plans have provided another talking point. The company is listed at Booth 138, with a 20-by-30-foot space, for the Dec.12- Dec.15 American Society of Hematology (ASH) meeting in New Orleans. Major exhibitors include Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Merck, AbbVie and Bristol Myers Squibb. The booth size has fueled speculation about a partnership or acquisition. Currently, investors are awaiting data from Sellas’ two lead programs. The Phase 3 Regal trial is testing GPS, an immunotherapy targeting WT1, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients who achieved a second complete remission following salvage treatment. Its final-analysis process is triggered by 80 deaths. Sellas reported 78 events as of May 11. Reaching 80 precedes database lock, data review and analysis before results are disclosed. The company also expects fourth-quarter topline data from its 80-patient Phase 2 SLS009 study in newly diagnosed AML, including patients with early resistance to azacitidine and venetoclax. SLS009 is also being explored in pancreatic cancer. Preclinical findings from last month showed 17.9% apoptosis (programmed cell death) in a patient-derived tumor model resistant to Daraxonrasib, versus 2.8% with Daraxonrasib alone. (AVGO) reversed overnight losses to edge up 0.3% late Monday as a 10-year cloud agreement with NTT Docomo did little to ease retail skepticism, with traders seeking a recovery catalyst after CEO Hock Tan’s AI “casino” remarks. AVGO stock rose nearly 2% on Monday to close at $334.59, snapping three straight sessions of losses. Broadcom extended its 2019 deal with Docomo, in which the companies will align their long-term tech roadmaps to advance the private cloud underpinning the Japanese telecom operator’s digital services. The company called it Broadcom Japan’s first “comprehensive” 10-year agreement covering VMware software licenses, technical assistance and maintenance support. Financial terms were not disclosed. VMware Cloud Foundation will be at the core of the infrastructure. The deal targets three priorities: keeping services available during system upgrades, strengthening security and resilience, and accelerating the delivery of new services. Docomo will use the platform to expand capacity and manage traffic spikes, improve security patching and anomaly detection, and run virtual machines and containers on a common platform. Automation across development, testing and releases will help shorten the time needed to introduce new features. The companies also plan to expand AI-driven operations and prepare the infrastructure for future developments, including 6G and IOWN. The agreement comes a week after Tan’s comments at a Singapore panel, where he called capital the biggest constraint on further AI development as Broadcom works through wafer and memory shortages. “A lot of investors have no clue what they're investing in, but set very extreme expectations, only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino gambling,” Tan said when asked about cheaper AI models, Reuters noted. His remarks addressed investment into the broader AI sector. Tan also acknowledged that Anthropic and OpenAI had shown an ability to generate significant revenue from their latest models deployed for AI personal assistants. SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk also subsequently responded, saying, “No crying in the casino,” weighing in on Tan’s concerns about speculative AI investments. Research and advisory firm Gartner recently said in a report that artificial intelligence infrastructure investments are in danger as concerns over bloated AI capex mount. The firm said that as the commercial duopoly for primary frontier models consolidates around Anthropic and OpenAI, the cash flows to meet that massive computing asset base from neoclouds are not scaling proportionally with upfront costs. Meanwhile, major Wall Street analysts are also taking opposing stances on CoreWeave. MoffettNathanson and BNP Paribas lowered their price targets on CoreWeave, while Goldman Sachs took a more positive outlook. MoffettNathanson slashed CRWV stock’s target to $89 from $107 and kept a ‘Neutral’ rating on the shares, citing its “staggering financial obligations.” BNP Paribas also cut its price target on CoreWeave to $117 from $169 and maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating, according to The Fly. The firm said that it sees a continued deterioration in investor confidence amid its debt obligations. While higher financing costs could contain the company's ability to fund future growth, the shares are "seemingly discounting some liquidity concerns," the analyst reportedly said in a research note. However, Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to ‘Buy’ from ‘Neutral’ and set a price target of $106, implying upside of more than 73% from its last close. The firm said ongoing volatility in the credit market raises questions about whether CoreWeave can finance its next phase of growth, and at what pace. However, Goldman also said the ongoing debate over demand for frontier vs. off-frontier intelligence, and CoreWeave's annual recurring revenue per megawatt and unlevered internal rate of return, are "biased to the upside" over the next 24 months because of tight supply. title: Chevron vs. ExxonMobil: Which Stock Has the Edge at 52-Week Highs? - TradingView
content: Energy giants Chevron Corporation CVX and ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM are attracting investor attention as their shares approach 52-week highs. CVX trades at $226.68, near its 52-week high of $229.04, while XOM changes hands at $178.23 against a high of $180.31. Rising crude prices have supported the stock’s recent gains, with Brent crude surging above $110 per barrel. Both companies benefit from oil and gas production, refining operations and disciplined capital allocation. However, buying near yearly peaks calls for examining whether operational improvements justify continued optimism. Their respective exposure to Guyana, the Permian Basin and downstream markets offers a common basis for comparing production growth, cash generation, operating efficiency and shareholder rewards. Chevron’s appeal centers on its enlarged upstream portfolio following the Hess acquisition. Second-quarter 2026 worldwide production reached 4.07 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, rising 20% year over year, aided by legacy Hess assets and growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America. Management expects full-year output of 3.98 million to 4.10 million barrels of oil equivalent per day. Its Guyana exposure also provides high-margin oil growth opportunities into the next decade. Cost discipline is another advantage. CVX achieved $1.5 billion in annualized Hess-related synergies, exceeding its original goal, while securing $3 billion in annual structural savings since 2024. These efforts can protect margins when commodity prices retreat. The company also expects to spend 25% less capital per barrel of oil equivalent in its U.S. shale and tight operations this year than last year, indicating stronger capital productivity. Chevron’s financial flexibility supports its investment appeal. It generated $22.6 billion in operating cash flow and $18.1 billion in free cash flow during the second quarter, while reducing total debt by $8.4 billion. A quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share and continued repurchases reinforce its shareholder-return focus. Moreover, a 20-year agreement to supply 2.67 gigawatts of power to a Microsoft data center creates an additional avenue for monetizing natural gas demand. Recent portfolio moves add promise and uncertainty. Agreements in Venezuela contemplate more than $7 billion of joint-venture investment over five years, with ambitions to more than double production to approximately 600,000 barrels daily. Separately, planned changes to Hess Midstream arrangements aim to halve Bakken unit midstream costs, although Chevron anticipates a substantial one-time accounting loss. Political exposure, execution risks and commodity sensitivity remain important considerations near the stock’s high. ExxonMobil brings greater operating scale and a broad portfolio spanning upstream production, fuels, chemicals and specialty products. Its second-quarter output totaled 4.51 million oil-equivalent barrels daily, despite Middle East disruptions. Production in the Permian exceeded 1.8 million barrels daily, and management sees a 9% compound annual growth trajectory there through 2030. In Guyana, the next floating production vessel is scheduled to add 250,000 barrels of daily capacity, reinforcing future supply growth. ExxonMobil’s integrated operations provide another differentiator. Record second-quarter diesel production demonstrated the value of refining capacity when supplies tightened, while chemical margins benefited from regional supply disruptions. Specialty products delivered particularly strong results. This combination gives XOM more ways to capture value beyond crude production, though refining and chemical earnings remain exposed to changes in product spreads and demand. Financial performance also stands out. XOM generated $23.6 billion in operating cash flow and $17.2 billion in free cash flow during the second quarter, alongside $14.7 billion in adjusted earnings. Shareholder distributions totaled $9.4 billion, split between $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in repurchases. Its declared quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share underscores a commitment to recurring cash returns. Efficiency initiatives strengthen ExxonMobil’s longer-term outlook. Cumulative structural cost savings have reached $16.3 billion, providing a platform for further margin improvement as high-value production expands. Still, aggressive capital spending, geopolitical interruptions and dependence on major project execution pose risks. With XOM trading close to its 52-week peak, investors must weigh its operational breadth and growth pipeline against expectations reflected in the share price. Year to date, shares of CVX and XOM have gained 48.8% and 48.2%, respectively. From a valuation perspective — in terms of forward price-to-sales ratio — ExxonMobil is trading at a similar valuation of 1.8X when compared with Chevron’s 1.89X. According to the Zacks Consensus Estimate, CVX’s earnings are set to rise 148.6% in 2026. The same for XOM’s 2026 EPS indicates a year-over-year increase of 95%. Both Chevron and ExxonMobil offer compelling investment opportunities, backed by strong production portfolios, healthy cash flows and consistent shareholder returns, justifying Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) for both companies. ExxonMobil benefits from its larger operating scale, diversified downstream businesses and expanding Permian and Guyana operations. However, Chevron appears better positioned for further upside. Its Hess acquisition, accelerating cost savings, improving capital efficiency and stronger free cash flow provide a solid foundation for future growth. Although both stocks have delivered nearly identical year-to-date gains and trade at comparable forward price-to-sales multiples, Chevron holds a clear advantage in earnings growth prospects. The Zacks Consensus Estimate projects 148.6% earnings growth for CVX in 2026, compared with 95% for XOM, making Chevron the more attractive investment choice. title: XOM vs. BP: Which Integrated Energy Giant Has the Edge? - The Globe and Mail
content: ExxonMobil Holdings CorporationXOM and BP plcBP are two integrated energy giants with promising business prospects, supported by the prevailing strength in crude oil prices. Investors’ strong preferences for both stocks are reflected in the price chart. Over the past year, XOM has jumped 53.6%, outperforming BP’s 42.5% surge. However, the stock price performance does not necessarily establish XOM's superiority over BP as an integrated energy company. Before arriving at an investment conclusion, let's examine the broader upstream business environment, which plays a crucial role in determining the cash flow potential of both energy giants. West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) crude is again approaching the $100-per-barrel mark, per Oilprice.com. The high prices are being driven by intensifying conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. Energy Information Administration, in its latest short-term energy outlook, projected WTI at $88.21 per barrel this year, higher than $65.40 last year. A highly favorable oil pricing environment is likely to continue supporting ExxonMobil’s exploration and production activities, as is likely for BP, a British energy giant. Importantly, upstream operations generate the majority of earnings for XOM. The company has a massive footprint in the Permian, the most prolific oil and gas play in the United States, and offshore Guyana. In the Permian, the integrated giant has been employing new drilling techniques and artificial intelligence to boost and optimize production volumes at lower cost structures. In Guyana, XOM has made several oil and gas discoveries, further highlighting its solid production outlook. Robust production from both assets has been aiding its top and bottom lines. Breakeven costs are low in both resources. Turning to BP, the British energy major’s production outlook looks bright, as its major projects, expected to begin operations between 2028 and 2030, are moving forward as planned. Once operational, these projects could help BP increase production and generate more cash. Although high oil prices are acting as a tailwind for the businesses of XOM and BP, it is also necessary to analyze the companies’ financial strength to judge how well the two energy majors could weather an unfavorable commodity pricing environment. The debt-to-capitalization of XOM is 13.73%, much lower than BP’s 43.29%. Thus, with significantly lower exposure to debt capital, ExxonMobil Holdings can sail through a tough business environment. BP, although having a relatively higher debt exposure, is also financially sound, as its debt-to-capitalization ratio is not very high. Coming to the valuation, BP stock is currently relatively cheap, as the integrated energy company is trading at a trailing 12-month EV/EBITDA multiple of 3.17x, which is lower than XOM’s 9.91x. In other words, investors are willing to pay a premium price for XOM over BP. The premium valuations reflect XOM’s strong business fundamentals, sound balance sheet and long-term growth prospects. Nevertheless, BP also presents a compelling investment case, given its relatively attractive valuation and the prevailing strength in crude oil prices, which should support its upstream profitability. With the barrel firm and the calendar set, the group has moved to the front of the sector conversation, and the figures it reports are expected to serve as an early marker for how the quarter unfolded across the broader complex. Crude has staged a forceful advance, with international and domestic benchmarks pushing into triple-digit territory on a blend of supply fears and firm demand. Each leg higher has drawn attention back toward the companies that pull barrels from the ground, since their earnings move closely with the prevailing price of oil. Market participants have pointed to a tightening of available supply, trimmed output from a producer alliance, and friction along key shipping routes as forces behind the climb. As a member of the S&P 500 and one of the heaviest weights in the energy group, Exxon Mobil has become a reference point whenever the barrel makes a decisive move, and the recent direction has been firmly upward. The strength of the move has also reshaped the tone across trading desks, where the barrel's climb has become a defining feature of the sector story. For a group whose top line tracks the oil price so closely, that momentum has translated into a steady stream of attention, and each fresh move in crude has reinforced the link between the commodity and the stock. The group also flagged, through a routine filing, that sequential movements in oil and natural-gas realizations and in refining margins would shape the quarter against the prior three-month stretch. Such snapshots are customary ahead of a major energy release, giving the market an early read on how price swings across crude, gas and refined products are likely to land. Midstream and downstream, it moves, refines and markets fuels, while a sizable chemicals arm converts hydrocarbons into plastics and other materials used across manufacturing. That breadth can steady the business through the cycle, because weakness in one link is often offset by strength in another. When crude softens, refining and chemical margins can widen as feedstock costs fall; when crude firms, the upstream arm captures the upside. This balance is a defining feature of the integrated majors and shapes how the market reads each quarterly release. The model also lets the group smooth the heavy capital demands of the business across its various arms, funding drilling in one period and refining upgrades in another. That flexibility, rooted in the scale and breadth of the operation, is part of what distinguishes the largest integrated majors from the narrower producers that populate the rest of the complex. The group's scale there lets it apply those techniques across a vast acreage position, compounding the gains and reinforcing the Permian's place at the core of the upstream story. With cash generation swelling during firmer-price stretches, attention turns to how the company allocates the proceeds. That approach gives the ownership base a direct link to the strength of the barrel while leaving room to fund drilling, refining upgrades and chemical projects. The coming figures are expected to update the market on the balance struck between distributions, the redeployment of cash across the business and the strength of the balance sheet, a mix that has defined the group's capital approach through the recent cycle. The steadiness of that record has long been a defining feature of how the market frames the group, distinguishing it from names with a more variable approach to cash paid out. That spread can move independently of the barrel, sometimes cushioning the group when crude softens. Both arms demand heavy capital and steady operational focus, and the market watches their margins closely as a counterweight to the swings of the upstream business. A firm tone to global demand, led by transport and industry, has reinforced the move. Currency swings add another layer, since crude is priced in dollars and a softer greenback can lift demand from outside the US. Geopolitical strain has periodically sent prices sharply higher, as any threat to the free flow of barrels tends to draw a swift market reaction. Together these threads have built a backdrop in which the barrel has pressed into triple digits, and the integrated majors have been among the clearest names in focus. Production volumes will show whether the upstream engine, led by the Permian, is delivering to plan, while realized prices will confirm how closely the group captured the firmer crude market. Refining and chemical margins will indicate whether the downstream arms are cushioning or amplifying the quarter. Beyond the figures, commentary on capital spending, the balance sheet and the cadence of distributions will shape how the market reads the group's direction. title: Is Exxon Mobil’s Next Big Thing Already Here? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock returned 63.1% over the past year, compared with 17.1% for the S&P 500. Further gains will need a fresh driver, and management named one during a July 31, 2026 call. Executives framed the asset as a turning point for Exxon’s cash. Which project is it, and what has changed there? That project is Exxon’s Guyana development, where the company has now earned back its investment. Management said during the July 31 call that the company fully recovered its $55 billion investment in the region, alongside all operating costs. Under the contract, up to 75% of production can go toward recovering that investment, and management said the remaining production is shared 50-50 with the government of Guyana. Guyana already operates at scale, pumping gross volumes of about 900,000 barrels a day during the second quarter of fiscal 2026. An analyst on the call asked whether the payback means more free cash flow or simply a smaller share of the oil. Management answered that it was “very much an inflection into free cash flow.” In the company’s view, the project has transitioned from paying back its cost to adding to Exxon’s cash. If you have held Exxon Mobil for years, your biggest question may be taxes, not the next catalyst. See how a tax-aware transition works. Guyanese operations fall under Exxon’s Upstream business. That unit generated $102 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025, compared with $324 billion for the entire company. The division also houses the Permian basin, where Exxon set a second-quarter production record of more than 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels a day. A payback event like the one in Guyana ultimately surfaces in cash generation. Exxon posted free cash flow of $17.0 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2026, up from $5.27 billion a year earlier. That single quarter accounted for more than half of the $30.6 billion the company generated over its last four quarters. Speaking about Guyana, management said it expects twice 2025’s level of free cash flow in 2030, and the company is evaluating a ninth FPSO, a floating production ship. Exxon stock finished trading on October 20, 2026, just 0.6% below its highest close of the past year. At that level, the shares traded at 22.7 times earnings over the past four quarters, tracking closely with the 23.0 multiple for the S&P 500. That four-quarter stretch includes the second quarter, which delivered $14.5 billion of the $32.8 billion Exxon earned. The primary doubt is how much of the second quarter’s cash stemmed from oil prices rather than from Guyana. Management said that market prices ran higher than base assumptions, generating more cash sooner. Executives also stated that the conflict in the Middle East affected Exxon’s operations there, and Exxon temporarily lost about 10% of its upstream production in the quarter. The next step in Guyana has a deadline. Exxon’s fifth FPSO, Errea Wittu, set sail toward Guyana in June and remains on track to start up by the end of 2026, management said. That leaves two things to watch: Exxon’s free cash flow in its third-quarter report, expected on or around October 30, 2026, and the start-up of Errea Wittu before the end of 2026.
